title: async/await & Structured Concurrency
scopeHtml: Scope: async/await, Task, TaskGroup, async let, cancellation, continuations, GCD vs Swift concurrency, comparison with Kotlin coroutines.

notes.title: Baseline and the mental model
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. In Android you write suspend fun, launch with viewModelScope.launch, fan out with async/coroutineScope, and cancel by cancelling a Job. In iOS the same ideas exist as async functions, Task, async let/TaskGroup, and Task.cancel(). The model is almost one-to-one, with different defaults.

Baseline: Swift 6 language mode, Xcode 16+, iOS 17/18 minimum. Swift concurrency back-deploys to iOS 13 with Xcode 13.2+ (verify for each newer API). Legacy forms (GCD, OperationQueue, completion handlers) are shown as "you will meet this in old codebases".

Android (Kotlin) iOS (Swift)
suspend fun f(): T func f() async throws -> T
call a suspend fun try await f()
viewModelScope.launch { } Task { } (inherits actor)
async { } / await() async let / TaskGroup
coroutineScope { } withTaskGroup / withThrowingTaskGroup
Job.cancel() task.cancel()
ensureActive() try Task.checkCancellation()
Dispatchers.Main @MainActor
Dispatchers.Default/IO the cooperative thread pool (no separate IO pool)
suspendCancellableCoroutine withCheckedThrowingContinuation
withTimeout none built in (use a task group race)
CoroutineContext element @TaskLocal
Flow<T> AsyncSequence / AsyncStream

Analogy, afterwards: coroutines on Android are a restaurant with waiters (dispatchers); Swift concurrency is the same restaurant, but a fixed number of waiters equal to the kitchen's stoves (CPU cores), and everyone must keep walking.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "async/await creates a new thread". It does not; it suspends and may resume on a different thread.
  • Assuming Task {} is like GlobalScope.launch; it is closer to scope.launch, inheriting actor and priority, but it is not structured (no automatic parent cancellation).
  • Quoting "Swift has no equivalent of Dispatchers"; actors and @MainActor take that role.

notes.title: async/await vs Kotlin suspend functions
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. A Kotlin suspend fun can only be called from another suspend function or a coroutine builder; the compiler rewrites it into a state machine with a Continuation parameter (CPS). Swift's async functions have the same rule and a similar transformation: an async function is split into partial tasks at every await, with the frame stored on the heap (async frame) instead of the thread stack.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
struct User: Decodable, Sendable { let id: Int; let name: String }

func loadUser(id: Int) async throws -> User {
    let url = URL(string: "https://api.example.com/users/\(id)")!
    let (data, response) = try await URLSession.shared.data(from: url)
    guard (response as? HTTPURLResponse)?.statusCode == 200 else {
        throw URLError(.badServerResponse)
    }
    return try JSONDecoder().decode(User.self, from: data)
}
suspend fun loadUser(id: Int): User {
    val resp = client.get("https://api.example.com/users/$id")
    check(resp.status.value == 200)
    return json.decodeFromString(resp.bodyAsText())
}

Differences that matter:

  • await marks every suspension point, like the (IDE-only) gutter icon in Kotlin, but it is mandatory in source. You can see where interleaving can happen.
  • Throws is separate. Kotlin suspend functions throw implicitly; Swift needs async throws and try await (order: try await).
  • Suspension does not hold a thread. While awaiting, the thread is returned to the pool. The code after await can resume on another thread (unless the function is isolated to an actor, which re-hops to it).
  • Entry from sync code: Task { await f() }. There is no runBlocking; blocking the main thread waiting for async work (semaphore) is a deadlock risk and a watchdog kill.
  • async properties and subscripts exist (var data: Data { get async throws }); async initialisers too.
  • Protocol requirements can be async; closures can be async (() async throws -> T).
  • @main struct App { static func main() async } is allowed for command-line tools.
  • Compiler/runtime: partial tasks are scheduled as jobs on an executor. A continuation (resume point) is allocated in the task's async frame, a bump allocated stack separate from the thread stack; deep recursion in async code is therefore far less likely to overflow the native stack.
  • Swift 6: values crossing isolation boundaries must be Sendable (see the actors note in this track).

Real industry usage: Apple's own APIs (URLSession.data(for:), PHPhotoLibrary, AVAsset.load(...), HealthKit, StoreKit 2 is async-first), Airbnb and Uber migrating from completion handlers and Combine to async/await, TCA effects via .run { send in ... }.

Analogy: an async function is a bookmarked reading: at every await you place a bookmark, put the book down (free the thread), and anyone (any thread) may pick it up where you left off.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing await blocks. It is a suspension point.
  • Forgetting try and await are separate checks; both are required at the call.
  • Calling async code from viewDidLoad without a Task (compile error) and then forgetting to cancel when the screen goes away.
  • Android vs iOS: Kotlin suspend functions are main-safe by convention; in Swift a non-isolated async function runs off the main actor (Swift 6 default for nonisolated async functions, see nonisolated(nonsending) below), verify the exact default per Xcode version.

notes.title: Task, Task.detached, priority and cancellation
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. viewModelScope.launch {} inherits the scope's dispatcher and cancels when the ViewModel clears. GlobalScope.launch is detached and discouraged. In Swift, Task { } inherits context and Task.detached { } does not; neither is cancelled automatically when the creating scope ends.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
@MainActor
final class ProfileViewModel {
    private(set) var user: User?
    private var loadTask: Task<Void, Never>?

    func onAppear() {
        loadTask?.cancel()
        loadTask = Task {                      // inherits @MainActor, priority, task-locals
            do {
                user = try await loadUser(id: 1)
            } catch is CancellationError {
                // ignore
            } catch {
                print(error)
            }
        }
    }

    func onDisappear() { loadTask?.cancel() }
}
class ProfileViewModel : ViewModel() {
    var user by mutableStateOf<User?>(null)
    private var loadJob: Job? = null

    fun onAppear() {
        loadJob?.cancel()
        loadJob = viewModelScope.launch {
            try { user = loadUser(1) }
            catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e }
            catch (e: Exception) { Log.e("VM", "fail", e) }
        }
    }
}

Which to use:

API Inherits actor Inherits priority Inherits task-locals Cancelled by parent
Task { } yes yes yes no (unstructured)
Task.detached { } no no (explicit) no no
async let / TaskGroup.addTask no actor (nonisolated) yes yes yes (structured)
SwiftUI .task { } @MainActor yes yes yes (view lifetime)

Priorities: .userInitiated, .high, .medium, .low, .utility, .background. They map onto QoS classes. Priority escalation: awaiting a lower priority task from a higher one boosts the awaited task. Thread priority inversion is mitigated by the runtime.

Cooperative cancellation:

  • task.cancel() sets a flag. Nothing stops automatically; the work must check.
  • Task.isCancelled (Bool), try Task.checkCancellation() (throws CancellationError), Task.currentPriority, withTaskCancellationHandler(operation:onCancel:) for immediate reaction (e.g. cancel a legacy network request).
  • Many system APIs (URLSession.data, Task.sleep, AsyncSequence iteration) are cancellation aware and throw CancellationError or URLError(.cancelled).
  • Cancelling a parent cancels all structured children, which each decide when to stop.
  • Task.value and Task.result let you await the outcome; an unhandled throw inside an unstructured Task is only visible through those. Swallowed errors from fire-and-forget tasks are a common production bug.
func renderThumbnails(_ ids: [Int]) async throws -> [Image] {
    var result: [Image] = []
    for id in ids {
        try Task.checkCancellation()         // cooperative check inside CPU loops
        result.append(try await makeThumb(id))
    }
    return result
}

let data = try await withTaskCancellationHandler {
    try await legacyDownloader.fetch(url)
} onCancel: {
    legacyDownloader.cancelAll()             // runs immediately on cancel, any thread
}

SwiftUI: .task { await vm.load() } starts when the view appears and is cancelled when it disappears; .task(id: query) { } cancels and restarts when id changes. This replaces the manual loadTask bookkeeping above for most screens.

Use Task.detached rarely: heavy CPU work that must not inherit @MainActor (though a nonisolated async function achieves the same, and is preferred). Its closure must capture only Sendable values.

Incident patterns: a search box starting a new Task per keystroke and never cancelling the previous one yields out-of-order results; fix with a stored task handle or .task(id:). An unbounded Task {} in a loop of 10,000 items spawns 10,000 tasks (cheap, but blow your server).

Analogy: cancel() is hanging a "please wrap up" sign on a worker: a polite worker checks the sign between jobs; one who never looks keeps working.

Common interview traps.

  • "Does cancelling stop the work?" Only cooperatively; CPU loops must check.
  • Believing Task {} created inside a view's method is cancelled when the view disappears (only .task does that).
  • Treating CancellationError as an error to show the user.
  • Android vs iOS: Kotlin cancellation is an exception you must rethrow; Swift cancellation is also a thrown error but swallowing it with try? is the same mistake.

notes.title: async let and TaskGroup vs coroutineScope and async
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. In Kotlin you run work in parallel with coroutineScope { val a = async { ... }; val b = async { ... }; a.await() + b.await() }. Swift offers async let for a fixed number of children, and TaskGroup for a dynamic number.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
func loadHome() async throws -> Home {
    async let profile = loadProfile()          // starts immediately, child task
    async let feed = loadFeed()
    async let banners = loadBanners()
    return try await Home(profile: profile, feed: feed, banners: banners)
}
suspend fun loadHome(): Home = coroutineScope {
    val profile = async { loadProfile() }
    val feed = async { loadFeed() }
    val banners = async { loadBanners() }
    Home(profile.await(), feed.await(), banners.await())
}

Rules for async let:

  • Child tasks start immediately. You await the variables later (the try can be at the await).
  • If the scope exits without awaiting, the child is implicitly cancelled and awaited (no leak), which is structured concurrency.
  • If one child throws and you await it, the others are cancelled when the function exits via the thrown error; you do not get Kotlin-style immediate sibling cancellation until you await/exit.

TaskGroup for a variable number:

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
func loadAll(ids: [Int]) async throws -> [User] {
    try await withThrowingTaskGroup(of: User.self) { group in
        for id in ids {
            group.addTask { try await loadUser(id: id) }
        }
        var users: [User] = []
        for try await user in group {          // completion order, not input order
            users.append(user)
        }
        return users
    }
}
suspend fun loadAll(ids: List<Int>): List<User> = coroutineScope {
    ids.map { async { loadUser(it) } }.awaitAll()   // keeps input order
}

Facts:

  • Results arrive in completion order. To keep order return (index, value) and sort, or collect into a dictionary.
  • If any child throws and the error propagates out of the group body, the group cancels all remaining children and the error is rethrown.
  • group.cancelAll(), group.addTaskUnlessCancelled, group.next(), group.waitForAll(), group.isEmpty.
  • Bounded concurrency (important: 500 images must not fire 500 requests): seed the group with N tasks then add one per completion.
try await withThrowingTaskGroup(of: Void.self) { group in
    var iterator = urls.makeIterator()
    for _ in 0..<4 {                                   // 4 at a time
        if let url = iterator.next() { group.addTask { try await download(url) } }
    }
    while try await group.next() != nil {
        if let url = iterator.next() { group.addTask { try await download(url) } }
    }
}
  • withDiscardingTaskGroup / withThrowingDiscardingTaskGroup (Swift 5.9, iOS 17+; verify back-deployment) for fire-and-collect-nothing, long-lived groups such as servers; finished children are freed immediately.
  • Child task closures are @Sendable: they cannot capture mutable local vars; collect results in the parent loop (as above), not inside the children.
  • Swift 6.1 / Xcode 16.3 added addTask improvements and typed-throws support on groups (verify).

Real industry usage: image grid prefetchers (Nuke, Kingfisher use their own queues but have async APIs), concurrent API calls on app launch (config, flags, profile), batch uploads with a cap on parallelism, Uber-style parallel feature-flag prefetch.

Analogy: async let is ordering three fixed dishes at once and picking them up together; a task group is a catering hall where the number of dishes depends on the guest list, with plates arriving as soon as each is ready.

Common interview traps.

  • Expecting TaskGroup results in submission order.
  • Putting await inside the async let declaration (async let x = await f() is wrong: the right side is the async call, no await needed there).
  • Mutating captured state in addTask closures (Swift 6 data-race error).
  • Spawning thousands of unbounded children for network calls.

notes.title: Continuations: bridging callbacks to async
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. In Kotlin you wrap a callback API with suspendCancellableCoroutine { cont -> ... cont.resume(value) } (or callbackFlow for streams). In Swift use withCheckedContinuation / withCheckedThrowingContinuation.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
func currentLocation() async throws -> CLLocation {
    try await withCheckedThrowingContinuation { continuation in
        legacyLocationManager.requestOnce { result in      // old callback API
            switch result {
            case .success(let loc): continuation.resume(returning: loc)
            case .failure(let err): continuation.resume(throwing: err)
            }
        }
    }
}
suspend fun currentLocation(): Location = suspendCancellableCoroutine { cont ->
    legacyLocationManager.requestOnce(object : Callback {
        override fun onSuccess(loc: Location) = cont.resume(loc)
        override fun onError(e: Throwable) = cont.resumeWithException(e)
    })
    cont.invokeOnCancellation { legacyLocationManager.cancel() }
}

The golden rule: resume exactly once.

Mistake Result with Checked variant Result with Unsafe variant
Never resume task hangs forever; a leaked-continuation warning is logged at deinit hang, no diagnostics
Resume twice runtime trap/crash SWIFT TASK CONTINUATION MISUSE: ... tried to resume its continuation more than once undefined behaviour
  • Use withCheckedContinuation in development and release; the checking overhead is small. withUnsafeContinuation removes the checks (performance only, rarely worth it).
  • continuation.resume(with: result) accepts a Result.
  • Continuations are not automatically cancellable. Combine with withTaskCancellationHandler to cancel the legacy operation and still resume once. Careful about a race where onCancel and the callback both resume: guard with a lock or an actor-protected flag.
  • Delegate-based APIs (CLLocationManagerDelegate, UNUserNotificationCenter delegate) cannot be wrapped by one continuation per call safely if multiple callbacks arrive; store continuation(s) in an actor, or wrap events in an AsyncStream.

Streams from callbacks:

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
func locationUpdates() -> AsyncStream<CLLocation> {
    AsyncStream { continuation in
        let token = legacy.startUpdates { loc in continuation.yield(loc) }
        continuation.onTermination = { _ in legacy.stopUpdates(token) }
    }
}

for await loc in locationUpdates() { show(loc) }
fun locationUpdates(): Flow<Location> = callbackFlow {
    val token = legacy.startUpdates { loc -> trySend(loc) }
    awaitClose { legacy.stopUpdates(token) }
}

AsyncStream buffers (default unbounded; set bufferingPolicy: .bufferingNewest(1) to avoid memory growth) and supports one consumer iteration; AsyncThrowingStream allows failure. Apple frameworks now offer many async variants directly (NotificationCenter.notifications(named:), URLSession.bytes, Task.sleep), prefer them over hand-rolled bridges.

Real industry usage: wrapping Firebase's completion handlers, CLLocationManager delegates, CNContactStore, third-party SDKs (payments, ads) that have not moved to async; Swift compiler can auto-generate async versions of Objective-C methods with completion handlers (imports foo(completion:) as async).

Analogy: a continuation is leaving a phone number at a bakery: you promise to call exactly once when the bread is ready; calling twice or never both leave you stuck.

Common interview traps.

  • Resuming twice or never (the number one continuation bug).
  • Forgetting cancellation: the awaiting task is cancelled but the continuation never resumes, so the task never finishes.
  • Using a continuation where an AsyncStream is needed (multiple values).
  • Calling resume while holding a lock that the awaiting code needs.

notes.title: GCD, DispatchQueue and OperationQueue: legacy and migration
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. On Android the old tools were Handler/Looper, AsyncTask (deprecated), Executors and RxJava schedulers. iOS equivalents are Grand Central Dispatch (GCD) queues and OperationQueue. You will meet these in old codebases and inside SDKs.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
// Legacy GCD (you will meet this in old codebases)
DispatchQueue.global(qos: .userInitiated).async {
    let image = decode(data)                    // background
    DispatchQueue.main.async {
        self.imageView.image = image            // main thread
    }
}
// Legacy Android equivalent
Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor().execute {
    val bitmap = decode(data)
    Handler(Looper.getMainLooper()).post { imageView.setImageBitmap(bitmap) }
}

GCD vocabulary:

Concept Meaning
Serial queue one task at a time, FIFO; used as a lock (DispatchQueue(label:))
Concurrent queue many at once; .global(qos:)
sync / async block the caller / return immediately
QoS .userInteractive, .userInitiated, .default, .utility, .background
DispatchGroup wait for N tasks (enter/leave/notify)
DispatchSemaphore counting semaphore (dangerous in async code)
DispatchWorkItem cancellable block
DispatchQueue.main main thread queue
barrier flag reader/writer lock on a concurrent queue

OperationQueue adds dependencies (addDependency), maxConcurrentOperationCount, KVO state, cancellation, and subclassable Operation. It is still used for ordered, dependent pipelines (e.g. image processing) and by Core Data / NSPersistentContainer internals.

Migration map:

Old pattern Modern replacement
DispatchQueue.main.async { } await MainActor.run { } or @MainActor function
serial queue protecting state actor
DispatchGroup + notify async let / TaskGroup
DispatchSemaphore limiting concurrency TaskGroup with bounded seeding
OperationQueue dependencies await chain or TaskGroup
DispatchWorkItem.cancel() Task.cancel()
Timer / asyncAfter try await Task.sleep(for: .seconds(1))
completion handlers async + continuation wrapper

Dangers that cause real incidents:

  • Thread explosion: blocking GCD threads (semaphore waits, sync calls) forces the system to spawn more threads, up to 64 workers per process, and then starves; symptoms are hangs and a watchdog kill (0x8badf00d, "ate bad food") when the main thread is blocked during launch (about 20 seconds in the foreground launch scenario; verify exact thresholds, they vary by scenario).
  • DispatchQueue.main.sync from the main thread deadlocks instantly.
  • Priority inversion: a .userInteractive task waiting on a .background queue; Xcode's Thread Performance Checker reports it.
  • Never block in async code: Do not use DispatchSemaphore.wait() or DispatchGroup.wait() in an async context; Swift concurrency assumes forward progress and a blocked cooperative thread can deadlock the pool.
  • Mixed usage is fine: you can call await inside Task, and call GCD from async code for legacy work; Xcode's Swift 6 mode warns on Sendable capture violations in GCD closures.

Reading Instruments: the Swift Concurrency template shows tasks, actors and continuations; the Time Profiler and Thread States views show blocked threads; Xcode's Main Thread Checker reports UI calls off main; Xcode Organizer > Hangs shows hang rate from MetricKit.

Analogy: GCD is a set of lanes on a highway you manage yourself (you pick the lane and hope no one blocks it); Swift concurrency is a traffic controller that places cars where they fit.

Common interview traps.

  • Using a serial queue as a lock while ignoring that actors are the modern equivalent (and are reentrant).
  • Using DispatchQueue.main.async and @MainActor interchangeably; ordering and compile-time checks differ.
  • Wrapping sync calls in a Task to "fix" a deadlock.
  • Android vs iOS: Dispatchers.IO exists to absorb blocking work; Swift has no IO pool, so blocking calls on the cooperative pool are harmful. Use async APIs or a dedicated DispatchQueue for truly blocking code.

notes.title: Timeouts, retries and task-local values
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. Kotlin has withTimeout(5_000) { } and retry/retryWhen on Flow; CoroutineContext elements carry request-scoped data. Swift has no built-in withTimeout (as of Swift 6.x; verify any newer addition), so you write a race with a task group. @TaskLocal plays the role of a ThreadLocal/CoroutineContext element.

Timeout helper:

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
struct TimeoutError: Error {}

func withTimeout<T: Sendable>(
    _ duration: Duration,
    operation: @escaping @Sendable () async throws -> T
) async throws -> T {
    try await withThrowingTaskGroup(of: T.self) { group in
        group.addTask { try await operation() }
        group.addTask {
            try await Task.sleep(for: duration)
            throw TimeoutError()
        }
        defer { group.cancelAll() }               // cancel the loser
        return try await group.next()!            // first result or first error
    }
}

let user = try await withTimeout(.seconds(5)) { try await loadUser(id: 1) }
val user = withTimeout(5_000) { loadUser(1) }   // throws TimeoutCancellationException

Important: the operation only stops early if it is cancellation-aware (URLSession is). For network calls you can also set URLRequest.timeoutInterval or URLSessionConfiguration.timeoutIntervalForRequest (default 60s per request; resource timeout 7 days), which is simpler.

Retry with exponential backoff and jitter:

func retry<T>(
    maxAttempts: Int = 3,
    initialDelay: Duration = .milliseconds(500),
    isRetryable: (Error) -> Bool = { _ in true },
    _ operation: () async throws -> T
) async throws -> T {
    var delay = initialDelay
    for attempt in 1...maxAttempts {
        do { return try await operation() }
        catch where attempt < maxAttempts && isRetryable(error) {
            let jitter = Double.random(in: 0.8...1.2)
            try await Task.sleep(for: delay * jitter)       // throws if cancelled
            delay *= 2
        }
    }
    fatalError("unreachable")
}

(Duration * Double exists since Swift 5.7 / iOS 16; verify minimum OS, and note that catch where uses the implicit error.) Retry only idempotent operations, honour Retry-After, and never retry cancellation or 4xx other than 408/429. Task.sleep(for:) is cancellation-aware; the older Task.sleep(nanoseconds:) also throws on cancel but is the legacy spelling.

Debounce with a stored task:

@MainActor final class SearchModel {
    private var searchTask: Task<Void, Never>?
    func queryChanged(_ q: String) {
        searchTask?.cancel()
        searchTask = Task {
            try? await Task.sleep(for: .milliseconds(300))
            guard !Task.isCancelled else { return }
            await runSearch(q)
        }
    }
}

Task-local values:

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
enum RequestContext {
    @TaskLocal static var requestID: String = "none"
}

func handle() async {
    await RequestContext.$requestID.withValue("abc-123") {
        await work()                       // task-local visible here and in child tasks
    }
}
func work() async { print(RequestContext.requestID) }   // abc-123
class RequestId(val id: String) : AbstractCoroutineContextElement(Key) {
    companion object Key : CoroutineContext.Key<RequestId>
}
withContext(RequestId("abc-123")) { work() }

Rules: task-locals are inherited by child tasks (async let, TaskGroup) and by Task { }, but not by Task.detached and not through GCD hops (copied only by Task creation APIs; verify for DispatchQueue.async). Use them for tracing IDs, logging context and feature-flag scopes; not as hidden dependency injection. Swift Testing and swift-log / swift-dependencies use task-locals for per-test overrides.

Real industry usage: Sentry/Datadog trace propagation, Point-Free's swift-dependencies (task-local overrides), Vapor/Hummingbird request IDs, search-as-you-type debouncing in Spotify/Instagram style search screens.

Analogy: a timeout is a kitchen timer next to the cook; retry with backoff is calling a busy restaurant again after waiting longer each time; a task-local is a name badge every worker in the same order wears.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing Swift has withTimeout; it does not (verify newer SDKs).
  • A timeout wrapper whose operation ignores cancellation: the error fires on time but the work keeps running.
  • Retrying non-idempotent POSTs, causing duplicate orders/payments.
  • Expecting task-locals to cross into Task.detached.

notes.title: Main thread, threading model and the cooperative thread pool
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. Android has one main thread (Looper) and Dispatchers.Default (cores threads) plus Dispatchers.IO (up to 64). iOS has the main thread (run loop) and the cooperative thread pool: roughly one thread per CPU core, shared by all of Swift concurrency. There is no IO dispatcher.

App process
  Main thread  <---- @MainActor isolated code (main executor = main DispatchQueue)
  Cooperative pool: N threads (N ~ active cores)
        runs: partial tasks of async functions, actor jobs, task group children
  Other GCD threads: serial/concurrent queues (outside the pool)

Key properties:

  • Forward progress guarantee: a task running on a pool thread should never block that thread on something that needs another pool thread. A pool of 6 threads with 6 blocked semaphore waits starves all concurrency. Block only via await.
  • @MainActor is a global actor whose executor is the main thread. UI updates, @Observable view models read by SwiftUI, and UIKit types (UIView, UIViewController are @MainActor in the iOS 17+ SDK) live here. Swift 6 mode turns off-main UI access into compile errors.
  • Hopping: calling an @MainActor function from a nonisolated async function suspends and resumes on the main thread; each hop costs a context switch (microseconds). Don't ping-pong in tight loops: batch the UI update.
  • Nonisolated async functions historically ran on the global concurrent executor (off the caller's actor). Swift 6.2 changed direction: the nonisolated(nonsending) option and the "approachable concurrency" build settings (e.g. NonisolatedNonsendingByDefault, default-@MainActor isolation for app targets) make plain async functions run on the caller's actor. This is fast-moving, verify against your Xcode (16 vs 26) build settings before answering in an interview.
  • MainActor.assumeIsolated { } asserts you are already on main (crashes in debug if not); useful for old delegate callbacks known to run on main.
  • Task { @MainActor in ... } and await MainActor.run { } are the explicit forms.
  • CPU-heavy work: in a nonisolated function or a detached task so it does not block the main actor. A 200 ms synchronous loop inside a @MainActor function freezes scrolling: Instruments' Hangs instrument and Xcode Organizer flag hangs over 250 ms (hang) and "microhangs" over 100 ms.
  • Executors: SerialExecutor, TaskExecutor (Swift 6, Task(executorPreference:), verify), and custom actor executors are advanced; mention them if asked about running on a specific queue.

Comparison and checklist for an Android developer:

Question Android iOS
UI thread name main / UI thread main thread, @MainActor
Where does await resume? the same dispatcher the actor it was isolated to, else any pool thread
Blocking I/O OK on Dispatchers.IO use async APIs; no IO pool
Thread count IO up to 64 pool about core count
Strict data-race detection none (convention) compiler-enforced in Swift 6 (Sendable, isolation)
Hang detector ANR dialog (5 s input) watchdog kill, Hangs in Organizer

Production incident patterns:

  • A synchronous JSON decode of a 20 MB payload in a @MainActor view model: scroll hitch of 300 ms, visible in Organizer "Hangs".
  • DispatchSemaphore used to turn an async call into a sync one inside an async function: full pool starvation, app frozen, no crash report (watchdog 0x8badf00d if during launch).
  • Updating @Observable state from a background task before Swift 6: purple runtime warning "Publishing changes from background threads is not allowed" (Combine/ObservableObject era) or an EXC_BAD_ACCESS/UIKit "Main Thread Checker" report; Swift 6 makes this a compile error.

Real industry usage: Airbnb/Uber describe moving database and image decode off the main actor; Apple's own Photos and Core Data (NSManagedObjectContext.perform) remain queue-confined, so legacy and new models coexist; Core Data's perform { } also has an async form.

Analogy: the main actor is the single cashier, the pool is a fixed team of stock clerks equal to the number of shelves. If clerks stand waiting for each other at the door, the shop jams; await lets them step aside.

Common interview traps.

  • "How many threads does Swift concurrency use?" About the number of cores, not one per task.
  • Blocking the pool (semaphores, Thread.sleep, synchronous heavy I/O) inside async functions.
  • Assuming code after await is on the same thread as before.
  • Thinking @MainActor alone fixes data races for non-UI shared state; mutable state shared between tasks needs actors or Sendable values (see the next topic in this track on actors and Sendable).
  • Android vs iOS: assuming there is an IO dispatcher to offload blocking work.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• async/await is Kotlin suspend with mandatory await markers; it suspends without holding a thread and may resume on another.
  • Task {} inherits actor, priority and task-locals; Task.detached inherits nothing; .task {} in SwiftUI is cancelled when the view goes away.
  • Cancellation is cooperative: check Task.isCancelled / checkCancellation(), use withTaskCancellationHandler for legacy cancel hooks, never show CancellationError.
  • async let covers a fixed number of children, TaskGroup a dynamic number (results in completion order); bound concurrency by seeding N and adding one per completion.
  • withCheckedContinuation bridges callbacks: resume exactly once, wire up cancellation, and use AsyncStream for multi-value callbacks.
  • GCD and OperationQueue are legacy: map serial queues to actors, groups to task groups, main.async to @MainActor, and never block with semaphores in async code.
  • Timeouts are a task-group race (no built-in withTimeout); retry only idempotent work with backoff and jitter; @TaskLocal carries request context to child tasks.
  • Threading: one main actor, a core-count cooperative pool, no IO dispatcher; blocking the pool starves concurrency and triggers hangs or watchdog kills.
  • Unverified: per-Xcode defaults for nonisolated async isolation (Swift 6.2 approachable concurrency), TaskExecutor details, Duration * Double availability, DiscardingTaskGroup back-deployment, task-local propagation through GCD, exact watchdog thresholds (verify).
